title: Memory and Storage
text:
Computers hold data in two different places:

Memory (RAM) is a computer’s short-term working space. It holds whatever a program is using right now, and it is cleared when the program ends.
Storage is long-term space for files. Files stay in storage whether or not a program is using them.

A useful comparison is a desk and a filing cabinet. Storage is the filing cabinet, where everything is kept. Memory is the desk, where you spread out the materials you are working with. A bigger desk lets you work with more at once, but it does not make you work faster.
In R, objects in your environment occupy memory. Files saved to disk occupy storage. Loading a large dataset into R requires enough memory to hold it.

title: Memory and Storage
text:
Memory on Longleaf
Each node on Longleaf has its own memory, ranging from about 41 GB to nearly 3 TB. When a job runs, Slurm reserves part of one node’s memory for that job, based on the amount requested.
Several jobs can run on the same node at once, each using its own share of the node’s CPUs and memory.

title: Memory and Storage
text:
Why the memory request matters
The amount of memory a job requests affects whether it succeeds and how soon it starts:

Too little: if a job tries to use more memory than it requested, it will be stopped before it finishes.
Too much: requesting extra memory does not make code run faster. Unused memory sits idle, unavailable to other users, and a large request may wait longer in the queue for a node with enough free memory.

The goal is to request what the job needs, plus a reasonable margin. Module 4 shows how to check how much memory a finished job actually used.

title: Memory and Storage
text:
Where files live
All Longleaf nodes share the same storage. A file saved from the login node is available to a job running on a compute node, and output written by a job can be viewed from the login node afterward.
Longleaf provides a few kinds of storage:

Home directory: a small personal space for scripts, settings, and installed packages. It is backed up.
Personal work space: a larger personal space for data and results while research is in progress. It is not backed up.
Project space: storage shared by a research group, requested by a PI.

Module 3 covers where these locations are and how to move files to and from them.

title: Nodes
text:
A node is a single computer within the cluster. Each node has its own processors (CPUs, or cores) and memory.
Longleaf connects roughly 300 nodes, giving researchers access to far more computing power than any single machine can provide.

title: Nodes
text:
Login nodes and compute nodes
Nodes on Longleaf play two different roles:

Login nodes are where you arrive when you connect to longleaf.unc.edu. This is where you edit code, run basic commands, and submit jobs to the scheduler.
Compute nodes are where jobs actually run. You do not log in to them directly; the scheduler sends your work to them.

Many people are connected to the same login node at the same time, so running an analysis there slows the system down for everyone.

title: Nodes
section: What Longleaf’s compute nodes look like
text:
What Longleaf’s compute nodes look like
Longleaf’s compute nodes vary in size:

CPUs per node: from 8 to 384
Memory per node: from about 41 GB to nearly 3 TB
GPUs: some nodes include NVIDIA A100, L40S, L40, V100, or GTX 1080 graphics processors
Most common node: 48 CPUs and 355 GB of memory (99 nodes)

These correspond to the general-purpose, large-memory, and GPU nodes introduced in the Longleaf overview.

title: A Brief History of Computing at UNC
text:
UNC’s effort to acquire a digital computer began in 1951, when Kenan Professor of Mathematics and department chair William M. Whyburn wrote to Chancellor R.B. House. Whyburn had become interested in digital computing through conversations with mathematicians at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, where he worked as a consultant.
UNC began canvassing the campus for interest in 1952. By 1955, eight academic departments had expressed interest: Economics, Business Administration, Mathematics, Mathematical Statistics, Biostatistics, Psychology, Psychometrics, and Physics.
In 1959, UNC-Chapel Hill installed a Sperry Rand UNIVAC 1105 in the basement of Phillips Hall. It was one of the most advanced computers in existence at the time and represented a major institutional investment in scientific and administrative computing.



The UNIVAC 1105 at UNC-Chapel Hill.


The machine was so large and heavy that the floors of Phillips Hall had to be reinforced with steel beams before it could be installed.
The UNIVAC arrived with an important assignment: it was one of only four computers in the United States used to process data for the 1960 U.S. Census. UNC also envisioned uses beyond the census. The University’s new Computation Center was intended to support quantitative work across academic disciplines and help researchers “enlarge the boundaries of human knowledge.”

title: A Brief History of Computing at UNC
text:
The UNIVAC by the numbers

Cost: $2.4 million in 1959—approximately $24 million in 2022 dollars
Weight: 19 tons
Working memory: 36–54 kilobytes
Storage: 5 megabytes of magnetic-tape storage
Capacity: One single-threaded, non-interruptible job at a time

Although those specifications appear extremely limited today, the UNIVAC 1105 was a powerful and advanced machine by the standards of 1959.

title: A Brief History of Computing at UNC
text:
How people accessed it
The UNIVAC was a monolithic computer: one large, centralized machine rather than a collection of independently accessible computers.
Users could not log in, open programs, or interact with the machine directly. Only system administrators operated the computer, so users accessed its computing capabilities through those administrators.
The computer could process only one job at a time. Once a job began, it ran without interruption until it finished or failed. After the 1960 Census work was completed, the machine was used primarily by university departments and administrative units, including UNC Finance and UNC Human Resources.

title: A Brief History of Computing at UNC

text:
Compared with a personal computer today
For perspective, consider a current lightweight laptop with 16 gigabytes of memory, 512 gigabytes of storage, and a weight of approximately 2.7 pounds.

A laptop with 16 GB of memory has approximately 300,000 times as much working memory as the upper end of the UNIVAC’s reported memory.
A 512 GB solid-state drive holds approximately 100,000 times as much data as the UNIVAC’s 5 MB of tape storage. A single compressed photograph from a modern phone can occupy several megabytes—potentially most of the UNIVAC’s reported storage capacity.
At 19 tons, the UNIVAC was approximately 14,000 times heavier than a 2.7-pound laptop.

Queue rules and responsible requests
Every job runs in a partition, a group of nodes intended for a particular kind of work:








Partition
Used for
Maximum run time




general
Standard CPU jobs; suitable for most work
11 days

Interactive sessions, such as running a graphical program or debugging code

GPU partitions
Jobs that use a GPU

general is the default partition. UNC recommends not specifying --partition=general in a job request: leaving it out allows Slurm to place the job on an idle node in another partition.

title: Longleaf Overview
text:
Longleaf is UNC-Chapel Hill’s shared research computing cluster. It gives researchers access to computing power, memory, storage, and specialized software beyond what is typically available on a personal computer.
Rather than relying on a single machine, Longleaf brings together many computers and makes their resources available to researchers across the university.

title: Longleaf Overview
text:
Longleaf is UNC-Chapel Hill’s shared research computing cluster. It gives researchers access to computing power, memory, storage, and specialized software beyond what is typically available on a personal computer.
Rather than relying on a single machine, Longleaf brings together many computers and makes their resources available to researchers across the university.

title: Longleaf Overview
text:
Why use a computing cluster?
A computing cluster can provide:

more processors and memory than a personal computer
capacity for computations that are too large or numerous for a laptop
access to research software and specialized hardware
large working storage for research data
scheduling and job management for a shared system

title: Longleaf Overview
text:
High-performance and high-throughput computing
Two terms are commonly used to describe work performed on computing clusters:







High-performance computing (HPC)
High-throughput computing (HTC)




Focuses on completing one large computation quickly
Focuses on completing many computations over time


Often divides one calculation among processors or nodes working together
Often consists of independent serial or single-node jobs


Example: one large simulation
Example: applying the same analysis to many files or parameter combinations



HPC and HTC describe patterns of computing rather than entirely separate kinds of machines. A shared computing cluster may support both patterns.

title: Longleaf Overview
text:
Longleaf’s focus
Longleaf was designed with high-throughput and data-intensive research in mind. This includes work involving:

large numbers of serial or single-node jobs
substantial memory requirements
large datasets
frequent reading and writing of data

This design makes Longleaf useful for research in which the main challenge is the number, size, or resource requirements of the computations.

title: Longleaf Overview
text:
Computing resources
Longleaf includes different kinds of compute nodes for different kinds of work:

General-purpose nodes support many common research applications.
High-I/O nodes support work that reads or writes large amounts of data.
Large-memory nodes support analyses that must hold substantial amounts of data in memory.
GPU nodes support software that can use graphics processors for computation.

The available resources continue to change as the cluster evolves, so current hardware specifications should be checked in UNC Research Computing documentation when they matter for a project.

title: Longleaf Overview
text:
When might Longleaf help?
Examples relevant to psychology, statistics, and related fields include:

applying the same analysis to many participants, datasets, or files
fitting many model specifications
running bootstrap, permutation, or simulation studies
processing files that are too large for a personal computer
running an analysis that requires more memory than a laptop provides
using research software or GPU resources that are unavailable locally

title: Longleaf Overview
text:
A shared resource
Many researchers use Longleaf at the same time. Users describe the work they want to run and the resources it needs. A scheduler then determines when and where that work will run.
The next module explains the parts of a computing cluster and how jobs move from a user’s computer to a compute node.

2 · Prepare
Use the login node to organize files and describe the job.


3 · Schedule

title: The Scheduler and the Queue
text:
What is the scheduler?
Longleaf is shared by researchers across the University, so users do not choose a compute node themselves. Instead, they submit a request to a scheduler, which decides when and where each job runs.
Longleaf uses a scheduler called Slurm. According to UNC Research Computing, Slurm has three main functions:

giving users access to cluster resources for a period of time so they can run code
starting, running, and monitoring work on those resources
managing competition for resources by keeping a queue of pending jobs

title: The Scheduler and the Queue
text:
What is a queue?
When you submit a job, it goes into a queue, where it waits until Slurm dispatches it to run somewhere on the cluster.
Longleaf uses a fair-share approach to decide which waiting jobs run next. Fair-share balances access among users and groups, taking into account how much of the cluster each has used recently.

title: The Scheduler and the Queue
text:
What do you ask for?
A job request tells Slurm what the job needs: how many CPUs, how much memory, and how much time. Slurm then finds a compute node with that much free capacity and reserves it for the job. Module 4 shows how to write and submit these requests.

title: The Scheduler and the Queue
text:
Partitions
A partition is a group of nodes. Every job runs in a partition. Longleaf has CPU-only partitions for most work and GPU partitions for jobs that use a GPU.
If a job request does not name a partition, the job runs in the default partition, general, which suits most jobs.
